item.text: {"winner":"A","confidence":"high","summary":"A is materially closer to the frozen API contract and has safer retry-body handling, though neither patch is merge-ready without substantial scope reduction.","reasons":["A provides the exact required `Upload(...opts ...FilesOption)` signature; B instead introduces `AddFileOption`, directly violating the frozen public API.","A leaves non-seekable raw bodies streaming and unreplayable, while B eagerly buffers every unrecognized body, causing broad memory/latency changes for `Raw.Do`.","B silently ignores `io.ReadAll` failures in `makeBodyReplayable`; after a partial read it may send only the unread remainder, corrupting requests instead of propagating the source error.","A has stronger multipart and retry coverage, including repeated fields, replayability, validation, API errors, and both retry attempts' content."],"risks_a":["`Upload` duplicates `Add` request construction, decoding, and error handling instead of calling `FilesService.Add` as required.","It adds prohibited association fields/options and `NewFileWithFields` machinery rather than using `multipartbody.NewFile` directly.","It broadly changes raw request replay, content-length, and caller-body ownership semantics despite the contract's scope restrictions and requirement to preserve `Add` behavior unchanged beyond the requested API path behavior implied by the contract setup; more importantly this is unrelated machinery refactoring the contract forbids outright except as necessary, and Upload itself does not need it because NewFile is already replayable. This creates review and compatibility risk around all Raw.Do consumers. It also does not include the required source-reader failure test or a streamed-reader retry test specifically through `Upload`."],"risks_b":["Its `Upload` signature uses `...AddFileOption`, not the required `...FilesOption`.","It also bypasses `FilesService.Add` and adds prohibited association APIs plus an unnecessary multipart helper variant.","`makeBodyReplayable` globally and eagerly consumes arbitrary streams, can block indefinitely or allocate unbounded memory, and swallows read errors after consuming part of the source. This is particularly dangerous because it can send truncated data while returning no source-reader error from setup. It also changes broad `Raw.Do` behavior outside the task's intended scope. Like A, B lacks source-reader error coverage and a streamed-content retry test through `Upload`; B additionally does not test `Upload` retry at all."]}
